content.title: AP Calculus BC: Particle Motion Analysis
content.overview: Particle motion involves analyzing the position, velocity, and acceleration of an object moving along a line. Success in this topic requires understanding the relationships between derivatives, interpreting sign changes to determine direction, and distinguishing between displacement and total distance.
learning_objectives: Relate position, velocity, and acceleration using differentiation and integration.
Identify times when a particle changes direction based on velocity sign changes.
Determine if speed is increasing or decreasing by comparing the signs of velocity and acceleration.
Calculate total distance traveled by integrating the absolute value of velocity over a specific interval.

sections.title: The Kinematic Hierarchy
sections.content: In AP Calculus, motion is typically restricted to a single dimension (a line). The relationship between the three primary functions is defined by calculus: Position, $s(t)$, represents the location relative to an origin. Velocity, $v(t) = s'(t)$, represents the rate of change of position. Acceleration, $a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t)$, represents the rate of change of velocity. Units must remain consistent; for example, if position is in meters and time in seconds, velocity is m/s and acceleration is m/s².

sections.title: Direction and Speed Analysis
sections.content: A particle changes direction only when its velocity changes sign (from positive to negative or vice versa). Simply reaching $v(t) = 0$ is not enough; the particle must actually cross the axis. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, $|v(t)|$. To determine if speed is increasing or decreasing at a specific time $t$: if $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ have the same sign (both positive or both negative), the particle is speeding up. If $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ have opposite signs, the particle is slowing down.

sections.title: Displacement vs. Total Distance
sections.content:
Displacement is the net change in position, calculated as the integral of velocity: $\int_{a}^{b} v(t) dt = s(b) - s(a)$. Total distance is the sum of all paths traveled, regardless of direction. It is calculated as the integral of the absolute value of velocity: $\int_{a}^{b} |v(t)| dt$. To compute this manually, you must identify all times $t$ where $v(t) = 0$ within the interval, split the integral at those points, and take the absolute value of each resulting sub-integral.

![A flow chart showing the steps to calculate total distance: find velocity zeros, identify sign changes, split the interval, and integrate the absolute value of velocity.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/45d1721b-19e6-4f0f-a8e3-17dc04e037bd-1786519354633-439.webp)

worked_examples.question: A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $v(t) = t^2 - 6t + 5$ for $0 \le t \le 7$. (a) Find when the particle changes direction. (b) Is the speed increasing or decreasing at $t = 0$? (c) Find the total distance traveled on $[0, 7]$.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Find direction changes. Set $v(t) = (t-1)(t-5) = 0$. Zeros are at $t=1$ and $t=5$. Testing intervals: for $t < 1$, $v(t) > 0$; for $1 < t < 5$, $v(t) < 0$; for $t > 5$, $v(t) > 0$. Since $v(t)$ changes sign at both $t=1$ and $t=5$, the particle changes direction at these times.

Step 2: Analyze speed at $t=0$. $v(0) = 5$ (positive). Acceleration $a(t) = v'(t) = 2t - 6$. $a(0) = -6$ (negative). Since $v(0)$ and $a(0)$ have opposite signs, the speed is decreasing.

Step 3: Calculate total distance. Split the integral at $t=1$ and $t=5$: $\int_{0}^{7} |v(t)| dt = |\int_{0}^{1} v(t) dt| + |\int_{1}^{5} v(t) dt| + |\int_{5}^{7} v(t) dt|$. 
Using the antiderivative $F(t) = \frac{1}{3}t^3 - 3t^2 + 5t$:
$F(1)-F(0) = 7/3$
$F(5)-F(1) = -32/3$
$F(7)-F(5) = 32/3$
Total Distance = $7/3 + |-32/3| + 32/3 = 71/3$ meters.

common_mistakes: Assuming a particle changes direction every time $v(t) = 0$. You must verify a sign change using a sign chart.
Confusing 'velocity is increasing' with 'speed is increasing'. Velocity increases when $a(t) > 0$, but speed only increases if $a(t)$ and $v(t)$ share the same sign.
Calculating displacement when the question asks for total distance.
Forgetting to include units (e.g., m/s or meters) in the final justification.
exam_tips: Always justify speed behavior by explicitly stating the signs of both $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ at the given point.
When using a calculator for total distance, use the absolute value function inside the integral: $\int |v(t)| dt$.
If asked for the position at time $t$, remember to add the initial position: $s(t) = s(0) + \int_{0}^{t} v(x) dx$.
content.recap: Particle motion requires a clear understanding of the derivative chain from position to acceleration. To analyze movement, use velocity sign charts for direction and compare velocity/acceleration signs for speed. For distance, always integrate the absolute value of velocity, splitting the interval at every point where the particle stops and turns.

knowledge_claims.content: Velocity $v(t)$ is the first derivative of position $s(t)$, and acceleration $a(t)$ is the first derivative of velocity $v(t)$.
A particle is moving to the right (or up) when $v(t) > 0$ and to the left (or down) when $v(t) < 0$.
A particle changes direction only at times $t$ where $v(t) = 0$ and $v(t)$ changes sign.
Speed is the absolute value of velocity, $|v(t)|$, and is a scalar quantity rather than a vector.
Speed is increasing at time $t$ if $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ have the same sign.
Speed is decreasing at time $t$ if $v(t)$ and $a(t)$ have opposite signs.
Displacement over the interval $[a, b]$ is the definite integral of velocity from $a$ to $b$.
Total distance traveled over the interval $[a, b]$ is the definite integral of the absolute value of velocity, $\int_{a}^{b} |v(t)| dt$.
To calculate total distance without a calculator, split the integral at every $t$ where $v(t)$ changes sign and sum the absolute values of the resulting integrals.
If $a(t) > 0$, the velocity of the particle is increasing, regardless of whether the speed is increasing.
When finding position $s(t)$ from velocity, the initial condition $s(0)$ or $s(t_0)$ must be added to the definite integral of velocity.
It is a mistake to assume speed is increasing simply because acceleration is positive; velocity must also be positive for this to be true.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Particle Motion — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Particle Motion: Position, velocity, speed, and acceleration are connected through derivatives, and direction changes occur when velocity changes sign.
options.B: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem: The Fundamental Theorem connects accumulation, antiderivatives, and net change and provides methods to evaluate definite integrals.
options.C: Initial Conditions and Euler's Method: An initial condition selects one solution from a family, and Euler's method advances by repeatedly using slope times step size.
options.D: Parametric Derivatives: For a parametric curve, dy/dx is the quotient of derivatives with respect to the parameter when dx/dt is nonzero.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Position, velocity, speed, and acceleration are connected through derivatives, and direction changes occur when velocity changes sign. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Particle Motion — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Antiderivatives and Substitution: Antiderivatives reverse differentiation, and substitution recognizes a composite integrand paired with an inner derivative.
options.B: Particle Motion: Position, velocity, speed, and acceleration are connected through derivatives, and direction changes occur when velocity changes sign.
options.C: Exponential Growth and Decay: When a rate of change is proportional to the current amount, the solution is exponential and its constant is determined by contextual data.
options.D: Second Derivatives of Parametric Curves: A parametric second derivative differentiates dy/dx with respect to the parameter and divides by dx/dt again.

items.explanation: Choice B is best because Position, velocity, speed, and acceleration are connected through derivatives, and direction changes occur when velocity changes sign. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.
